content: Congenital syphilis is caused by the bacterium Treponema pallidum, which is transmitted to the fetus in utero from an infected mother via the placenta. The severity of the disease depends on the stage of maternal infection and the duration of fetal exposure. Transmission typically occurs during the second trimester, with the highest rates of transmission observed in women with primary syphilis. The risk of transmission decreases as the duration of maternal infection increases, due to a reduction in the concentration of spirochetes in the bloodstream. Fetal infection can result in stillbirth, miscarriage, or live birth with severe manifestations such as hydrops fetalis. Prenatal screening for syphilis during the first trimester is recommended for all pregnant women, and adequate treatment with penicillin effectively prevents transmission to the fetus. Congenital syphilis was first described in a 17th-century English pediatric textbook. Transplacental transmission from an asymptomatic infected mother was first documented in 1906. Sir Jonathan Hutchinson identified a diagnostic triad for congenital syphilis, consisting of notched incisors, interstitial keratitis, and eighth cranial nerve deafness. Congenital syphilis is classified into early (presenting within 0–2 years) and late (presenting after 2 years) forms based on the time of clinical presentation. A diagnostic classification is also used for surveillance purposes. The risk of fetal transmission is influenced by the stage of maternal disease, which correlates with the concentration of spirochetes in the bloodstream, and the duration of fetal exposure. Vertical transmission risk is highest in untreated mothers with primary syphilis (70–100%), decreases to 40% in early latent syphilis, and further declines to 10% in late latent syphilis. This variation is attributed to the decreasing spirochete concentration in maternal blood over time. Congenital syphilis is caused by Treponema pallidum, which is transmitted from mother to child during fetal development or at birth. Routine antenatal screening for syphilis is recommended. Infants with congenital syphilis may present with symptoms such as failure to gain weight or thrive, fever, irritability, small blisters on the palms and soles, and watery nasal discharge. Physical examination findings suggestive of congenital syphilis include low birth weight, signs of prematurity, skin edema, pleural effusion, vesicular skin rash, corneal clouding, jaundice, and deafness. Antenatal ultrasound findings indicative of congenital syphilis include hydrops fetalis (characterized by scalp edema, placental thickening, serous cavity effusion, and polyhydramnios), hepatosplenomegaly, placentomegaly, non-continuous gastrointestinal obstruction, and small bowel dilation. Postnatal diagnosis can be made by examining the placenta or umbilical cord using silver staining to detect spirochetes or by performing a T. pallidum PCR test. The treatment for neonates presenting with symptoms of congenital syphilis is aqueous penicillin G. However, the evaluation and management depend on the specific clinical scenario at presentation. Primary prevention measures include routine syphilis screening in pregnant women, individuals with high-risk behaviors, and those living in areas with high prevalence. Additional measures include abstinence from intimate contact with infected individuals, consistent use of latex condoms, limiting the number of sexual partners, avoiding the sharing of sex toys, and practicing safe sex. Secondary prevention involves regular follow-up of infants with congenital syphilis to monitor for the reappearance of signs and symptoms after recommended treatment, which has been shown to improve outcomes.
